class.name: PhysXFlow3D
class.brief_description: NVIDIA Flow smoke, fire and dust, provided by the PhysX module.
class.description: Simulates gas with NVIDIA Flow: a sparse, unbounded grid (it grows wherever the gas goes) with pressure projection, vorticity confinement and combustion. It's fed by the [PhysXFlowEmitter3D] nodes whose [member PhysXFlowEmitter3D.flow] points at it (or, with none set, by every emitter when this is the scene's only [PhysXFlow3D]); physics bodies within [member collision_range] of those emitters are solids the gas flows around, and moving bodies push it. Flow runs on Godot's own [RenderingDevice] (Vulkan or Direct3D 12), and [PhysXFlowRenderEffect] draws it into the frame with Flow's own ray marcher, self-shadowed by the scene's first visible [DirectionalLight3D] -- straight from the GPU, at the simulation's full resolution. Nothing is read back to the CPU unless [member cpu_readback] is on. The render effect is installed by itself, without touching anything you save: with no [Compositor] in the world one is created on the [World3D] while flows exist, and a [Compositor] of your own (on a [WorldEnvironment] or [Camera3D]) gets the effect added at the rendering-server level only -- its effects array is never modified. All of it is undone when the world's last flow leaves. [b]Requirements:[/b] an engine built with [code]flow_sdk=[/code], [code]nvflow.dll[/code] and [code]nvflowext.dll[/code] next to the executable (they are loaded at run time -- without them this node shows a warning and stays inert), and the Forward+ or Mobile renderer (not Compatibility, not headless). Flow's shaders are compiled the first time each is used (a fraction of a second on a first run) and kept in Godot's shader cache folder. [b]Units:[/b] meters and m/s, like the rest of the scene; Flow's own tuned defaults are converted at the boundary.

method.name: get_stats
method.description: Diagnostics: [code]running[/code], [code]error[/code], [code]start_ms[/code] (grid creation), [code]step_ms[/code], [code]render_calls[/code], [code]render_outputs[/code], [code]readback_bytes[/code], [code]bounds[/code] (the gas, with [member cpu_readback]), [code]active_blocks[/code] (sparse blocks in use, of [member max_blocks]), [code]scatter_lights[/code] / [code]scatter_passes[/code] / [code]scatter_no_source[/code] (see [member light_scattering]: lights picked last step, scattering passes run, frames Flow had no volume to hand over), and Flow's pipeline / pass / resource counts.

method.name: is_running
method.description: Whether Flow is running for this node (see the configuration warnings if not).

method.name: sample_smoke
method.description: The smoke at [param position] (world space), from the last CPU readback. Needs [member cpu_readback]; returns [code]-1.0[/code] without it. The readback lags a few frames behind the simulation.

method.name: sample_temperature
method.description: The temperature at [param position] (world space), from the last CPU readback, in the same units as [member PhysXFlowEmitter3D.temperature], [member ignition_temperature] and [member temperature_range] -- e.g. how much a fire hurts or how hot a sensor reads. Needs [member cpu_readback]; returns [code]-1.0[/code] without it. The readback lags a few frames behind the simulation.

members.member: Upward acceleration per unit of temperature: hot gas rises, cool gas hangs. "Up" is opposite the project's default gravity.
Simulation cell size in meters. Smaller is finer detail and more GPU cost.
Physics bodies near the gas become solids for it. Box, sphere, capsule and cylinder shapes are supported; convex, concave and heightmap shapes are not yet.
The physics layers whose bodies the gas collides with.
How far from this flow's emitters (in meters) bodies are looked for. With [member cpu_readback] on, the area the gas has spread to is searched as well.
Fuel burns when hotter than [member ignition_temperature], releasing heat and smoke.
How fast the gas cools (exponential, per second).

Copy temperature and smoke back to the CPU every few steps, for [method sample_smoke], [method sample_temperature] and the [code]bounds[/code] in [method get_stats]. Off by default: it costs a full field copy each time and isn't needed for rendering.
How bright the [member heat_ramp] glow is. [code]0[/code] turns glowing off.

When enabled, gas never goes below [member floor_height]: a wide solid lies under it (it reserves no blocks and holds no gas). Colliders can't describe terrain heightmaps or trimeshes, so without a floor gas sinks into the ground and spends the grid's blocks there.
The world height of the floor's top (used when [member floor_enabled] is on).

How the gas glows by temperature, from [code]0[/code] to [member temperature_range]: each color is the glow at that temperature, its alpha how much it glows instead of showing the lit smoke. Empty uses a built-in fire ramp (transparent when cool, deep orange when warm, yellow-white when hot).
The temperature above which fuel burns (see [member combustion]).

When enabled, nearby [OmniLight3D] and [SpotLight3D] nodes light the gas: each glows in the smoke in its own color, fading with distance the way it fades on surfaces (its [member OmniLight3D.omni_range] / [member SpotLight3D.spot_range], [member OmniLight3D.omni_attenuation] / [member SpotLight3D.spot_attenuation], spot cone), dimmed by the gas between it and each point and by the gas in front of the camera. Flow's own renderer lights the gas with the scene's first [DirectionalLight3D] the same from every side; with [member scattering_directional], directional lights scatter here too. This is an extra pass over the pixels the gas covers, so it's off by default. Up to [member scattering_max_lights] lights are used, the strongest at the gas first. Each light's [member Light3D.light_volumetric_fog_energy] scales its glow, as it does for Godot's volumetric fog: set it to [code]0[/code] to keep a light out of the gas.

The most sparse blocks the gas may take up -- a GPU memory budget, since Flow reserves memory for all of them when the grid starts (about 0.45 MB a block: the default 1024 is roughly 0.5 GB). A small plume uses a few hundred; [method get_stats] reports [code]active_blocks[/code]. Gas that would need more is cut off, with a warning. Changing it restarts the simulation.

With [member light_scattering], how much the gas scatters light forward (toward a camera looking at the light) rather than evenly in every direction: [code]0[/code] glows the same from every side, higher values make a bright halo when looking toward a light, negative values light the gas most when the light is behind the camera.

With [member light_scattering], the scene's [DirectionalLight3D] nodes scatter in the gas too, on top of Flow's own sun lighting (which is the same from every side): with [member scattering_anisotropy] above [code]0[/code], gas between the camera and the sun glows, brightest where it's thin -- dust or smoke lit from behind. Each one's [member Light3D.light_volumetric_fog_energy] scales its glow. The gas shades it (up to [member scattering_shadow_reach] toward the light); scene objects don't yet. Off by default: a scene's sun would otherwise add a glow to all its gas.
With [member light_scattering], the most lights that glow in the gas at once (the strongest at it). Each one costs a short march toward it for every step of every pixel the gas covers.

With [member light_scattering], which kinds of light have their glow in the gas blocked by scene objects: each point reads the light's own shadow (the one Godot already renders for meshes, so only for lights with [member Light3D.shadow_enabled]), the way Godot's volumetric fog does, so pillars in front of a light cast dark shafts through the gas. One shadow lookup per shadowed light per step; untick a kind to save it. (The [DirectionalLight3D] already shades the gas through the gas itself; its scene shadows aren't read yet.) To light the gas from inside an object (a lamp in a glowing block), keep the object from shadowing its own light: put it on a render layer of its own and leave that layer out of the light's [member Light3D.shadow_caster_mask].

With [member light_scattering], the resolution the glow is worked out at. Scattered light and its shadows in a gas are soft, so [constant SCATTERING_RESOLUTION_QUARTER] (the default) reads the same as full at about a sixth of the cost; the result is scaled up depth-aware, so the glow doesn't bleed onto the edges of objects in front of the gas. [constant SCATTERING_RESOLUTION_HALF] or [constant SCATTERING_RESOLUTION_FULL] sharpen the edges of the shadows in the glow, for close-ups.
With [member light_scattering], how far (in meters) each point looks toward a light for gas that dims it. Beyond that, gas between a point and the light is ignored.

With [member light_scattering], the steps of the march toward each light that lets the gas shade itself (a light inside thick smoke glows near it and dims further in). [code]0[/code] skips it: cheaper, but light then reaches every point as if through clear air.
With [member light_scattering], a multiplier on the light the gas scatters. The glow is colored by [member smoke_color].

How far the self-shadowing reaches toward the light, in steps of three quarters of a cell (48 is about 1.8 m at the default [member cell_size]). Too few for the gas's width leaves it lit almost evenly. [code]0[/code] turns self-shadowing off.
The smoke's color, lit by the scene's sun: white steam, gray or black smoke, brown dust, colored signal smoke. See also [member smoke_ramp].
Opacity per meter, per unit of smoke. Burning fuel makes a lot of smoke, so fire reads dense at the default; plain smoke or dust emitters may want 2-10.
How fast smoke thins out (per second). Lower values let it climb and linger longer.

The smoke's color by temperature, from [code]0[/code] to [member temperature_range] -- e.g. black soot near a fire turning light gray as it cools. Empty uses [member smoke_color] at every temperature. Alpha is ignored (opacity comes from the smoke itself).
The temperature at the end of [member heat_ramp].
Vorticity confinement: keeps small swirls alive for rolling, billowing gas.

constants.constant: The glow is worked out for every pixel.
Half the resolution each way (a quarter of the pixels), scaled up depth-aware.
A quarter of the resolution each way, scaled up depth-aware.
[OmniLight3D] shadows block their glow in the gas.
[SpotLight3D] shadows block their glow in the gas.
